name: Kuul (Horn of Africa kohl)

card.summary: A traditional dark eye cosmetic from Somali, Ethiopian, Eritrean and Djiboutian communities that outlines and darkens the eyes for a defined, lengthened-lash look.
card.note: Traditional kohl can contain lead; the US FDA considers it unsafe.

quick.overview:
Kuul is the Somali word for kohl, the dark eye cosmetic traditionally made from ground minerals or charred plant material. In the Horn of Africa it is applied along the lash line to darken and define the eyes; the phrase indha kuul means kohl eyes.

Kohl use in the region is described as reaching back to the ancient Kingdom of Punt. Besides beauty, users say it cleans the eyes, lengthens lashes and shields from sun. Research on kohl generally has focused on lead content rather than cosmetic outcomes.
quick.how: It is applied as a fine line to the lid margin, traditionally with a small stick or applicator. Recipes vary and may be made at home or bought, with modern versions using carbon or charcoal.
quick.risks: Some traditional kohl contains lead sulfide (galena); studies in the early 1990s found very high lead in some preparations, and use has been linked to higher blood lead levels, though other studies dispute the link. The US FDA considers kohl unsafe and does not allow its import or sale.

lead: Kuul is the term for kohl used by Somali speakers and communities across the Horn of Africa, including Djibouti, Ethiopia and Eritrea [1]. Wikipedia reports that women in these regions have long worn it to darken the eyes, with use traced back to the ancient Kingdom of Punt [1].

For appearance, kuul outlines and defines the eyes and visually lengthens the lashes; users also say it cleans the eyes and protects them from sunlight [1]. Kohl overall is traditionally ground from stibnite (antimony sulfide), though many traditional and commercial versions use galena (lead sulfide) or charcoal and soot [1].

angle.text: Kuul is a pigment applied along the lids to make the eyes look darker and more defined. Users describe it as a cosmetic that also cleans and protects the eyes.

paras: Recipes for kohl vary by region. In North Africa and the Middle East homemade kohl is often galena, while Western manufacturers use amorphous carbon or charcoal mixed with plant oils and soot from nuts, seeds or resins [1]. Some lead-free versions are regarded by users as inferior, which has sustained demand for traditional preparations [1].

Kohl has been worn in Egypt since about 3100 BCE, originally to protect against eye ailments and possibly sun, and evidence from Nubia suggests Bronze Age use there [1]. In the Horn of Africa its use is dated to the Kingdom of Punt [1].

Studies in the early 1990s found lead at up to 84 percent in some commercial kohl, and kohl use has been linked to higher blood lead levels, which can cause anemia and developmental effects; other studies dispute the links [1]. A 2016 Pakistan study of surma found inhalation and exposure risks from lead-containing product [1]. The US FDA considers kohl unsafe because of potential lead content [1].
No studies found. Related research on kohl in other regions has examined lead content and blood lead levels, as above [1].
